en: The Sūtra on the Measure of Merit of the Rare and Wondrous, translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of the Sui Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.
At that time, the elder bhikṣu Ānanda was sitting alone in a forest hermitage, reflecting and thinking to himself:
"If good sons and good daughters are able to receive and uphold the three refuges, making this declaration:
'I now take refuge in the Buddha, I take refuge in the Dharma, I take refuge in the Saṃgha.'"
"How much merit would one obtain?

Having formed this thought, at the time when the sun first rose, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat in his dwelling, adjusted his robes, and proceeded with composed dignity to where the Buddha was.

Having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!
Just now, while in a secluded place, I reflected thus:
"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were able to say:
'I now take refuge in the Buddha, I take refuge in the Dharma, I take refuge in the Sangha.'"
"How much merit does one obtain?
I truly do not understand; I only pray that the Tathāgata will analyze and explain this, so that all sentient beings may attain right knowledge and vision.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!
You, son of good family, possess true wisdom that is subtle and capable of excellent deliberation; you are able to ask the Tathāgata about such a meaning as this.”
As you have reflected, if those sons or daughters of good family can purify their minds by giving rise to such a thought:
"I now take refuge in the Buddha, I take refuge in the Dharma, and I take refuge in the Saṅgha."
"As for the amount of merit one attains, listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well!
I shall analyze and explain it for you."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
"So be it, World-Honored One!"
"I wish to hear it with joy.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:

"This land of Jambudvīpa is seven thousand yojanas in length and breadth; its shape is like a carriage box, narrow in the south and broad in the north. Suppose it were filled with stream-enterers (srotāpanna), as densely as bamboo, reeds, sugarcane, rice, or hemp."

Suppose there are good men and good women who, for a full hundred years, provide all manner of worldly articles of entertainment to all such stream-enterers; furthermore, they fully provide the four requisites to support, honor, and prostrate before them; and even after their parinirvāṇa, they collect their relics and erect stupas made of the seven precious substances, making offerings to each and every stupa and temple with incense, flowers, ghee, oil, lamps, candles, music and dance, silken fabrics, banners, canopies, and various other offerings.
"What do you think?
Would those sons or daughters of good family acquire much merit?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
“Very many,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
“Ānanda! It is not as good as if a son or daughter of good family, with a pure and sincere heart, were to speak these words:
‘I now take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṅgha.’”

The merit thus obtained cannot be matched by that previous merit even by a hundredth part, nor by a thousandth part, nor by a hundred-thousand-millionth part; indeed, it is beyond the reach of calculation or analogy.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Ānanda:
"Set aside Jambudvīpa for a moment.

Suppose there were Aparagoyānī, eight thousand yojanas in length and breadth, its shape like a half-moon, and it were entirely filled with Sakṛdāgāmins, as densely packed as bamboo, reeds, sugarcane, rice, or hemp."

If there are good men or good women who, for a full two hundred years, provide the four worldly requisites as previously described, and even after his parinirvāṇa, collect his relics and erect stupas made of the seven precious substances, and to each and every stupa offer various kinds of worship with flowers, incense, lamps, music, silk canopies, banners, and streamers.
"What do you think?
Would that son or daughter of good family acquire much merit?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:
"Very much so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
“Ānanda! It is not as good as this:
if a son or daughter of good family, with a pure and sincere mind, should speak these words:
‘I now take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṅgha.’”

The merit thus obtained is such that the aforementioned merit does not equal even one hundredth part of it, nor one thousandth part, nor one hundred-millionth part, nor one hundred-thousand-billionth part; indeed, it cannot be reached by any calculation or analogy.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Ānanda:
"Set aside for a moment one Jambudvīpa and one Aparagoyānī.

Suppose, furthermore, that Pūrvavideha in the east were nine thousand yojanas in length and breadth, its terrestrial shape like a full moon, and it were entirely filled with Anāgāmins, as densely as bamboo, reeds, sugarcane, rice, or hemp."

If there are good men or good women who, for a full three hundred years, again provide offerings of all four requisites and every kind of pleasurable thing as before, and even after his parinirvāṇa, collect his relics and erect stupas made of the seven precious substances, making various offerings to each and every stupa with flowers, incense, music, banners, and canopies.
"What do you think?
Would that son or daughter of good family acquire much merit?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
“Very many,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
“Ānanda! It is not as good as when a son or daughter of good family, with a pure and sincere mind, speaks these words:
‘I now take refuge in the Buddha, I take refuge in the Dharma, and I take refuge in the Saṅgha.’”

The merit thus obtained cannot be compared to that previous merit: it does not equal even one hundredth part, nor one thousandth part, nor one hundred-thousandth part, nor one ten-millionth part, nor one billionth part, nor one hundred-billionth part, nor one trillionth part; indeed, it is beyond all calculation or analogy.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Ānanda:
"Set aside for a moment one Jambudvīpa, one Aparagoyānī, and one Pūrvavideha."

Suppose that in the north, in Uttarakuru, which is ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth, with its terrain square, straight, and perfectly symmetrical on all sides, were filled with arhats—those whose outflows are exhausted, who are free from further afflictions, who have attained mastery over their minds, who possess right liberation, who have attained liberation through right knowledge, whose minds are well-tamed, who are great dragons among men, who have accomplished what was to be done, who have laid down the heavy burden, who have attained their own benefit, and who will not undergo further existence; whose holy life is established, whose bodies and minds are unimpeded, who understand the intentions of sentient beings, and who have attained the six supernormal powers and the eight liberations, as densely as bamboo, reeds, sugarcane, rice, or hemp.

If there are good sons or good daughters who, for a full four hundred years, further provide offerings and show respect through the four requisites, providing all articles of pleasure as before, and even after their parinirvāṇa, erect stūpas made of the seven precious substances, and to each individual stūpa they offer various kinds of worship with flowers, incense, music, lamps, canopies of silk, banners, and streamers.
"What do you think?
Would those sons or daughters of good family acquire much merit?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
“Very much so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
“Ānanda! It is not as good as this:
if a son or daughter of good family, with a pure and sincere mind, should speak these words:
‘I now take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṅgha.’”

The merit thus obtained does not equal even one hundredth part of the former merit; it does not equal one thousandth part, nor one hundred-thousandth part, nor even one hundred-thousand-billionth part; indeed, it cannot be reached by any calculation or analogy.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Ānanda:
"Set aside Jambudvīpa, Aparagoyānī, Pūrvavideha, and Uttarakuru for now."
Suppose that throughout the four continents, there were *pratyekabuddhas*—solitary realizers—filling them as densely as bamboo, reeds, sugarcane, rice, or hemp.

If a son or daughter of good family were to provide for them for ten thousand years with the four requisites of service, honoring and respecting them while supplying all articles of pleasure as previously described, and even after their parinirvāṇa, were to collect their relics and erect stūpas made of the seven precious substances, and to honor each individual stūpa with flowers, incense, music, lamps, canopies, banners, and various other offerings.
"What do you think?
Would that son or daughter of good family acquire much merit?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
“Very much so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
“Ānanda! It is not as good as this:
if a son or daughter of good family, with a pure and sincere mind, should speak these words:
‘I now take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṅgha.’”

The merit thus obtained cannot be matched by the former merit even in a hundredth part, nor in a thousandth part, nor in a hundred-thousandth part, nor in a hundred-thousand-billionth part; indeed, it is beyond the reach of calculation or analogy.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Ānanda:
"Set aside for a moment a single four-continent world, the area illuminated by the light of one sun and moon.

Suppose there were a thousandfold world-system—namely, a thousand suns and moons, a thousand great oceans, a thousand Sumeru Kings of Mountains, a thousand Jambudvīpas, a thousand Aparagoyānīs, a thousand Pūrvavidehas, a thousand Uttarakurus, a thousand heavens of the Four Great Kings, a thousand Trāyastriṃśa heavens, a thousand Yāma heavens, a thousand Tuṣita heavens, a thousand Nirmāṇarati heavens, a thousand Paranirmita-vaśavartin heavens, and a thousand Brahmā heavens—each independent and not mutually connected, such that each attains great sovereignty within its own thousand worlds."
Ānanda! This is called a small chiliocosm. Ānanda!
When one counts from a single small thousand-world system until a full thousand have been reached, this is called a medium thousand-world system. Ānanda!
When one further counts from a medium thousand-world system, counting each one until a full thousand are reached again, this is called a great thousand-world system.
Ānanda! This total number of worlds combined is called a trichiliocosm.

Suppose the trichiliocosm were filled with Buddhas, Tathāgatas—just as with bamboo, reeds, sugarcane, rice, or hemp—such would be those Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, Arhats, Perfectly Enlightened Ones.

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, for twenty thousand years, constantly provide all manner of articles of entertainment—clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine—as various offerings, and even after his parinirvāṇa, collect his relics and erect stupas made of the seven precious substances, and to each and every stupa offer worship with flowers, incense, music, silken canopies, banners and pennants, fragrant candles, and oil lamps.
"What do you think?
Would those sons and daughters of good family acquire much merit?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:
“Very much so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If there were someone who could simply make offerings to a single Buddha, the World-Honored One, for twenty thousand years—providing the four requisites with full devotion and respect, and even after his parinirvāṇa, collecting his relics and erecting stūpas made of the seven precious gems, each of which they honor by offering flowers, incense, music, banners, canopies, fragrant oils, and lamps—their merit would still be vast, immeasurable, boundless, and beyond calculation; how much more so if it were done for all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, filling an entire trichiliocosm!"

For twenty thousand years, they constantly provided offerings and support with the four requisites until his parinirvāṇa; thereafter, they collected his relics and erected stūpas made of the seven precious substances. To each individual stūpa, they offered flowers, incense, music, banners, canopies, fragrant oils, lamps, and all manner of necessary items. Thus, they truly attained an immeasurable, boundless, unreckonable, and incalculable mass of merit.
The Buddha said:
“Ānanda! It is not even equal to this:
when a son of good family or a daughter of good family, with a pure and sincere mind, speaks these words:”

"If one now takes refuge in the Buddha, takes refuge in the Dharma, and takes refuge in the Saṃgha, the merit obtained will surpass the previous merit by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, or ten-thousandfold; it cannot be calculated, nor can it be known through words or analogies."
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Ānanda:

"If there is anyone who can take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṅgha, and who is able to undertake the ten wholesome actions for even as long as a finger-snap, and having undertaken them, practices them accordingly—by this cause and condition, they shall obtain immeasurable and boundless merit."

“Ānanda! If there is another person who, for one day and one night, having received the eightfold precepts (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa), practices according to the teaching, the merit they obtain surpasses the previous merit by a thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, a hundred-thousand-ten-thousandfold, even to the point that it cannot be reached by calculation or analogy.”

“Ānanda! If one can receive and uphold the five precepts for as long as life lasts and practice according to the teachings, the merit obtained will surpass the previous merit by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, and even a hundred-thousand-ten-thousand-millionfold; it cannot be reached by calculation or analogy.”

“Ānanda! If there were another person who received the śrāmaṇera precepts or the śrāmaṇerī precepts, it would surpass the former by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, or even a hundred-billionfold—beyond what can be known through calculation or analogy.”

“Ānanda! If there should be another person who is able to receive and uphold the śikṣamāṇā precepts, the merit they obtain will surpass the previous merit by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a hundred-thousand-millionfold, even to the point that it cannot be reached by calculation or analogy.”
How much more so for one who upholds the Bhikṣuṇī precepts and practices according to the instructions of the Prātimokṣa!

How much more so for someone who, throughout their entire life, upholds the great Bhikṣu precepts and practices according to the instructions of the Prātimokṣa precepts—without deficiency, without transgression, and free from defilement—maintaining pure Brahma-conduct and attaining immeasurable and boundless merit that surpasses the former by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, or even a hundred-thousand-ten-thousandfold, to the point that it cannot be reached even by calculation or analogy.

At that time, the Elder Ānanda, having heard the Buddha speak of these three refuges and how the merit of observing the Prātimokṣa of a great bhikṣu for as long as life lasts is immeasurable, marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How extraordinary!
"Bhagavān!
This sutra is subtle and inconceivable, elucidating most profound meanings; its merit is vast and difficult to measure.
What should this sutra be named?"
"How should we receive and uphold it?
The Buddha told Ānanda, "The name of this sutra is 'The Sutra of the Rare and Unprecedented'; you should receive and uphold it."
Why is this so? Because this sutra speaks of rare dharmas; the sublime dharmas it expounds are difficult for all the worlds to hear, and for this reason they are called "rare."
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the Elder Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Measurement of the Merit of the Rare and Marvelous.
